questions.q: What distinguishes an infinite game from a finite game?
a: It has no defined end, and players aim to keep playing
It has fixed rules that never change
It always produces a clear winner and loser
It can only be played by large companies
questions.why: Lesson 1 says infinite games have no beginning or end and the goal is to stay in the game.

questions.q: What happens when an infinite game is played with a finite mindset?
a: Problems arise, as with FIFA's short-term World Cup decision
The game becomes fairer for new players
The rules eventually stop changing altogether
Everyone involved benefits over the long run
questions.why: Lesson 1 says trouble comes from finite thinking, and cites FIFA's Qatar choice and the fan backlash.

questions.q: Which trait must a Just Cause have, according to the summary?
a: It must benefit someone other than the business itself
It must be achievable within a few years
It must appeal mainly to the company's investors
It must focus on beating a named competitor
questions.why: Lesson 2 lists being service-oriented, with someone besides the business as the main beneficiary.

questions.q: What does it mean for a Just Cause to be 'for' something rather than 'against' something?
a: It fights for a positive outcome, not just an enemy
It names a rival that must be defeated
It avoids taking any public position
It changes with each new market trend
questions.why: Lesson 2 contrasts fighting for every human's right to eat with fighting against famine.

questions.q: What is a Worthy Rival, per the summary?
a: A competitor whose strengths you can learn from
A rival you must drive out of the market
A partner who shares your profits
A mentor who has already retired
questions.why: Lesson 3 describes a Worthy Rival as someone whose skills you can study and improve from.
